candidates.attacker_control: The step argument `job` (BuildTriggerStep.job, line 35; resolved at BuildTriggerStepExecution.java:61-62) is supplied by the pipeline script. In common forwarding patterns it is derived from user-influenced data (build parameters such as `params.TARGET`, an `input` step, a shared library, or a job that forwards user input), so a user with permission to run/parameterize the upstream pipeline can name an arbitrary existing item. The `parameters` argument (BuildTriggerStepExecution.java:82-86) is equally script/user-influenced.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) Jenkins Pipeline intentionally executes approved scripts with the pipeline author's trust, so the absence of a check may be by design, not a defect; literal job names in an approved script are author-chosen. (2) Freestyle-style downstream triggering ('Build other projects' post-build action) also does not require downstream Build permission, by design, because it is configured by someone with Configure on the upstream. (3) I could not inspect Jenkins core to determine whether `Jenkins.getItem(String, ItemGroup, Class)`, `ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2`, or `Queue.schedule2` perform hidden ACL filtering or whether an Authentication for the triggering user is available to an async step (core/workflow-step-api sources are not in this snapshot). (4) The snapshot has no tests, so intended behavior cannot be corroborated; the plugin's own error messages (Messages.properties:28-29) only cover 'No such job' and unsupported item types, not permissions. (5) The relation index contains only an `@Inject` navigation fact for this file (line 56) and no permission/ACL edge, so the index neither confirms nor refutes the missing check.
candidates.impact: Unauthorized build triggering: a user who can run an upstream pipeline can start builds of jobs they are not allowed to build (consuming executors/agents, publishing/deploying artifacts, causing downstream side effects), and can attach parameter values to those builds. Where downstream jobs are permission-restricted (e.g., production deploy jobs), the upstream pipeline becomes a privilege-escalation path rather than an enforcement boundary. Severity depends on deployment-specific RBAC and on whether the target name is user-influenced; with literal, author-controlled names the same code makes the upstream pipeline's author the effective authority for downstream builds.
candidates.prerequisites: Attacker can cause the upstream Pipeline job to run (or control the `job` value it passes to `build`), the referenced item exists, and the attacker lacks Build/Configure permission on it but has permission on the upstream job. The pipeline script/step must already be approved/executable by that user (sandbox or trusted-script boundary is assumed already crossed; this finding is about the missing item-level authorization inside the step).
candidates.root_cause: BuildTriggerStepExecution.start() resolves the target item purely by name from the pipeline-script-supplied step argument (`Jenkins.getActiveInstance().getItem(job, invokingRun.getParent(), Item.class)`, line 62) and then schedules it unconditionally via `ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2` (lines 92-97) or `Queue.schedule2` (line 131). No ACL/Authentication check for the downstream item exists anywhere in the plugin; the plugin does not pass any user identity for authorization, and the scheduling APIs used are the low-level, permission-free ones. This is inconsistent with the codebase's own practice of explicit permission checks elsewhere (Item.READ check in doAutoCompleteJob, BuildTriggerStep.java:151).
candidates.title: `build` step schedules downstream builds without any permission check on the target item
candidates.trace: script `build job: <attacker-influenced name>` -> BuildTriggerStep.job (BuildTriggerStep.java:35,42-48) -> BuildTriggerStepExecution.start() line 61-62 gets the step argument and resolves the Item by name with getItem(..., Item.class); line 66-69 only rejects wait+non-Job; lines 70-97 (ParameterizedJob path) or 101-134 (Queue.Task path) build Actions (Cause.UpstreamCause, and ParametersAction when parameters are supplied) and call scheduleBuild2/schedule2 with no ACL lookup; lines 142-147 return/complete. Nothing in this path consults Authentication/ACL or Item.BUILD; a repository-wide search for `hasPermission` returns only the Item.READ check in the autocompletion UI helper (BuildTriggerStep.java:151).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Unverified: (a) whether a per-user Authentication is available inside the step and what permission (Item.BUILD vs Item.READ) would be the correct requirement; (b) whether core or the scheduler enforces any ACL on the paths used; (c) whether upstream Jenkins considered downstream-trigger authorization out of scope; (d) the exact upstream fix/commit, if any, corresponding to this snapshot (no web/ground-truth access; version 2.6-SNAPSHOT, deps jenkins 1.642.3 / workflow-support 2.6 / workflow-step-api 2.3).

rejected_leads.lead: Runtime build parameters are not validated against the downstream job's defined parameters, unlike the UI/snippet path: `DescriptorImpl.newInstance` (BuildTriggerStep.java:92-118) resolves `ParametersDefinitionProperty` and rejects unknown names ('No such parameter definition'), but `BuildTriggerStepExecution.start()` (lines 82-86) and `completeDefaultParameters` (lines 150-171) attach a `ParametersAction` built from script-supplied ParameterValue names/types with no validation or filtering, and no check that the job is parameterized at all.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible 'arbitrary build parameters' (SECURITY-170 class), and the in-repo asymmetry is good evidence; kept as a lead, not the primary candidate because the parameter names/values are supplied by the approved pipeline script (author-controlled), the UI-path validation exists for snippet generation, and I could not confirm that filtering is expected at runtime or that upstream changed this behavior. Same root region as the chosen candidate; not submitted separately per the one-candidate cap.

rejected_leads.lead: `doAutoCompleteJob` relative-path loop (BuildTriggerStep.java:173-184): for a crafted `value` consisting largely of '../' in a non-root context, `container = ((Item) container).getParent()` can yield null or a non-Item root (Jenkins), then `new Visitor(p).onItemGroup(container)` can NPE/ClassCastException, producing a request error.
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker-controlled query parameter exists, but impact is limited to a UI error/DoS for the requesting user; item enumeration is gated by the Item.READ check at line 151. Not a strong security finding.

rejected_leads.lead: Form-validation endpoints `doCheckJob` / `doCheckWait` (BuildTriggerStep.java:202-231) resolve arbitrary item names via `Jenkins.getActiveInstance().getItem(value, context, Item.class)` and return distinguishable responses ('No such job {0}', 'Building a {0} is not supported', OK) without an explicit permission check.
rejected_leads.reason: At most minor existence/type disclosure for users who can reach the descriptor's form validation; impact too weak relative to the chosen candidate, and core may constrain these endpoints.

rejected_leads.lead: `BuildTriggerAction.Trigger.context` (BuildTriggerAction.java:21-57) serializes the upstream StepContext into downstream queue items and run records; `stop()` cancels entire coalesced queue items (BuildTriggerStepExecution.java:188-198) and `maybeInterrupt` aborts whole downstream runs (lines 200-233) even when multiple upstreams share the folded item.
rejected_leads.reason: StepContext persistence is required for wait/resume and the action is an InvisibleAction not exposed in the UI/API; the coalesced-cancellation tradeoff is explicitly acknowledged in code comments (lines 191-193). No concrete sensitive-data access or tampering path was demonstrated from this snapshot.

summary: Snapshot is Jenkins Pipeline: Build Step plugin 2.6-SNAPSHOT (13 files: 5 Java sources, pom.xml, .gitignore, 4 help HTML + Messages.properties; no tests/CI files). I read every Java source completely (BuildTriggerStep.java, BuildTriggerStepExecution.java, BuildTriggerAction.java, BuildTriggerListener.java, BuildQueueListener.java, BuildTriggerCancelledCause.java), pom.xml, Messages.properties, and reconstructed the four help HTML files via search. The strongest plausible issue is that the `build` step schedules a downstream build through `BuildTriggerStepExecution.start()` without any authorization check on the resolved downstream item: the script-supplied `job` string is resolved only by name (`Jenkins.getActiveInstance().getItem(job, invokingRun.getParent(), Item.class)`) and then scheduled via `ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2` / `Queue.schedule2`; the plugin contains no ACL/Authentication check on the target item anywhere (the only permission call in the whole snapshot is `i.hasPermission(Item.READ)` in the autocompletion helper, BuildTriggerStep.java:151). A user who can run an upstream pipeline whose target job name is user-influenced (build parameter, `input`, shared library, forwarded `params`) can therefore trigger builds of jobs they are not permitted to build, and attach a `ParametersAction` to them. This is a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability: I could not verify whether Jenkins core or the runner silently enforces ACLs in `getItem`/`scheduleBuild2` (core sources are not in the snapshot), and Pipeline's design arguably treats the approved pipeline script as the authorization gate. The second-best lead (runtime parameter names/types not validated against the downstream job's `ParametersDefinitionProperty`, unlike the descriptor `newInstance` path) is listed as an unconfirmed rejected lead rather than a second candidate.
